analysis.one_liner: Narrows which illnesses qualify for unpaid family and medical leave and gives employers more say over it.
analysis.headline: The Senate took no vote on the bill; it died in committee after being referred there in March 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The Family and Medical Leave Act guarantees many workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for a serious health problem or a new child. This bill would have shrunk that guarantee: it excluded short-term illnesses from coverage, listed the conditions that still qualify, let employers require leave to be taken in four-hour chunks, added notice and paperwork deadlines that could cost workers their leave, and let employers force workers to choose between their paid sick leave and the law's unpaid leave instead of using both. It never advanced past the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers covered by the Family and Medical Leave Act. The bill's own findings say employers face administrative costs, paperwork, scheduling problems, and conflicts between the leave law and their own sick-pay policies [S3]. Narrowing the definition of a serious health condition, requiring four-hour minimum blocks of intermittent leave, and letting employers manage absences through their own plans would reduce unplanned absences and compliance costs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers covered by the leave law

how_it_helps.text: Excludes short-term illnesses and injuries with brief treatment and recovery from the definition of a serious health condition, and adds a specific list of conditions (such as heart attacks, strokes, childbirth, and pregnancy complications) that remain covered [S2][S3].

Lets employers require intermittent leave — leave taken a few hours or days at a time — to be taken in minimum blocks of four hours, and lets them require traveling employees to take leave for whole assignments [S2][S3].

Adds deadlines for workers to request leave: a written application within five working days of notice for foreseeable leave, and at least oral notice by the day leave starts for unforeseeable leave; a worker who misses the deadline can be denied leave [S2][S3].

Lets employers require an employee to choose between the law's unpaid leave and paid sick leave, sick pay, or disability pay under the employer's plans — meaning workers could no longer run both, with paid leave covering some weeks and unpaid leave covering the rest [S2][S3].
Directs the Labor Department to review all existing regulations carrying out the leave law and replace them within set deadlines [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who need leave. A worker with a serious-but-brief condition could lose coverage entirely. Workers using leave in small pieces, such as for chemotherapy or dialysis, could be forced into four-hour blocks. Workers who miss the new notice and paperwork deadlines could be denied leave. Workers relying on both paid sick time and unpaid leave would have to give up one, effectively shortening their total time away from work when they or a family member is seriously ill [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers needing family or medical leave

drawbacks.text: The bill responds to real employer complaints: its findings section describes significant administrative and personnel costs, lost productivity, scheduling difficulties, and paperwork burdens from the current law's broad regulations [S3]. An honest supporter would say employers with genuine family-friendly policies bear real compliance costs.

The exclusion for conditions where 'treatment and recovery are very brief' is undefined, leaving workers unsure whether a condition like a severe flu complication or short hospital stay qualifies, and giving employers room to dispute claims.

The forced choice between paid sick leave and unpaid leave would leave workers with less total protected time off than they have under current law, since paid and unpaid leave could no longer be combined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades predictability for employers against protection for workers. Employers would get clearer rules, fewer covered conditions, and more control over when and how leave is taken. Workers would lose coverage for some conditions, face new deadlines that could forfeit their leave, and see their combined paid-plus-unprotected time off shrink. The costs fall on people at some of the hardest moments of their lives — a serious diagnosis, a difficult pregnancy, a new child — while the savings accrue to employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in March 2001 and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2003 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Judd Gregg introduced the bill on March 8, 2001, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
One Senate Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee never reported the bill, and no committee vote, floor vote, or further action appears in the record before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who rely on family and medical leave are better off, since the protections they have today were never narrowed. Employers who wanted reduced leave obligations gained nothing from the bill's failure to advance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers relying on family and medical leave

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family and Medical Leave Clarification Act on March 8, 2001.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; never reported it to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, so the bill drew support only from one party's side, and no recorded opposition exists in the record.

industries.industry: Employers covered by the Family and Medical Leave Act
industries.note: The bill would have reduced employers' obligations: fewer covered conditions, four-hour minimum blocks of intermittent leave, stricter worker deadlines, and the right to make workers choose between paid sick leave and unpaid leave. The benefit to employers comes directly out of the leave protections workers hold today.
